title: Life Started Out Wet
question: How did the oceans shape the story of life on Earth?
hook: Long before anything grew on land, life was taking shape around vents on the deep sea floor.
idea: Life began in the oceans, spread from there into fresh water and onto land, and sea life still shapes the air and the shores.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in the early history of ocean life in order.
items: Simple microbes appear around deep-sea hydrothermal vents
The Great Oxygenation Event changes ocean chemistry
The Avalon Explosion of mostly fixed-in-place animals
The Cambrian Explosion of actively moving animals
beats.explain: The first microbes arose in Archean oceans, oxygen rose in the early Proterozoic, the Avalon Explosion came in the Neoproterozoic, and the Cambrian Explosion followed in the early Phanerozoic.

beats.prompt: Oxygen floods the ancient oceans, where the existing microbes live without it. What happens next?

choices.label: Nothing changes, since microbes ignore oxygen
choices.feedback: Tempting because microbes are tough, but the change in chemistry was severe enough to likely cause a widespread extinction.

choices.label: Many die out, but survivors team up into a new kind of cell
All life in the sea is wiped out for good
choices.feedback: Tempting given the scale of the shock, but some anaerobes survived and went on to form new life.

beats.explain: The Great Oxygenation Event likely caused a widespread anaerobe extinction, but it also led to eukaryotes through symbiogenesis between surviving anaerobes and aerobes.

beats.prompt: Match each kind of sea life to what it is known for.
pairs: Can be as small as 0.02 micrometres
Help create new land by building reefs
beats.explain: Marine life spans an enormous size range, and some groups reshape the planet itself, from the air to the land.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Marine vertebrates include saltwater fish, marine mammals, marine reptiles and seabirds.
Vertebrates tend to be active swimmers with high oxygen needs.
Marine invertebrates need even more oxygen than vertebrates do.
So when oxygen runs low, fish are among the first to die in large numbers.
beats.explain: Marine invertebrates are much more tolerant of low oxygen than vertebrates, with many adaptations for poorly oxygenated water.
